note: How the shared spine's CEFR stages line up with the language-specific proficiency exams a learner might actually sit. CEFR is the backbone because the spine already speaks it (core/spine.json declares pre-A1 through C2) and because most of the corpus's European tracks certify against it directly. Everything else maps ONTO CEFR rather than replacing it, so one level field serves every track and a 'ramp to A1' book is a filter, not a separate corpus.
everyTrackIsMapped: Every registered track has a mapping. Where no awarding body publishes a CEFR alignment, this file states the project's own editorial judgement rather than leaving a gap — a learner asking 'what is A1 in Tamil?' deserves an answer, and an unmapped track silently drops out of every level report. What is NOT negotiable is saying which kind of answer each one is: `basis` is `published` when the awarding body states the alignment, `research` when it is a widely-cited third-party correspondence, and `editorial` when it is this project's judgement. An editorial mapping is a working default to be corrected, never a claim about what a certificate is worth.
notePreA1: pre-A1 is NOT a CEFR level. CEFR begins at A1. It is this curriculum's own label for the ramp below A1 — the greetings-and-first-words stretch this project exists to make gentle — and it is exactly the material an exam syllabus assumes you already have. Naming it keeps the ramp measurable instead of invisible.

japanese.exam: JLPT plus Coding Adventures Japanese production companion

mapping.A2: JLPT N4 pass with total 90+, or N3 pass with total 95-103
mapping.B1: JLPT N3 pass with total 104+, or N2 pass with total 90-111
mapping.B2: JLPT N2 pass with total 112+, or N1 pass with total 100-141
mapping.C2: beyond the official JLPT CEFR reference range

japanese.caveat: Official JLPT score reports add these CEFR reference indications from the December 2025 test, but only for candidates who pass the named JLPT level and only for the language knowledge, reading, and listening competence JLPT tests. JLPT does not test production (speaking and writing) or interaction. The complete four-skill destination therefore pairs the published receptive anchor with a project-defined JF Standard/CEFR-aligned production companion; pre-A1 and C2 are wholly project-defined.

chinese.caveat: Hanban's own alignment for the six-band HSK. HSK 3.0 (2021) redefines the bands as nine levels and shifts the correspondence upward; revisit when the Chinese track passes HSK3 material.

arabic.caveat: Arabic certification is fragmented and diglossic: ALPT and the ILR/ACTFL scales test Modern Standard Arabic, while the corpus also teaches greetings a learner would hear in dialect. The mapping is for MSA.

persian.caveat: A straight six-to-six correspondence is this project's judgement, not AMFA's. The exam is administered chiefly for study in Iran and its bands are not published against CEFR descriptors, so treat the rungs as evenly spaced only until someone checks them.

hindi.exam: Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha ladder
hindi.caveat: A real and widely-sat ladder, but built to spread Hindi to non-Hindi-speaking India rather than to CEFR's can-do descriptors, so the rungs are not evenly spaced against CEFR. Judgement, offered as a working anchor.

urdu.caveat: Urdu shares its spoken core with Hindi, so the Hindi anchors above are the nearest reference; the script and the Persian-Arabic register are where the two diverge and where the ramp differs.

tamil.exam: no single international ladder; Singapore MOE Tamil and Tamil Nadu state syllabi are the nearest
tamil.caveat: The project's judgement, per the owner's instruction to map rather than leave gaps. Tamil's diglossia is the reason no mapping is clean: the written/literary register and the spoken register diverge sharply, and this curriculum teaches spoken Tamil first. Read A1 here as 'can greet, introduce oneself and handle a short exchange in spoken Tamil', which is the CEFR descriptor, not a claim about any Tamil examination.

marwadi.exam: Coding Adventures Marwadi Assessment — project-defined equivalent
marwadi.caveat: No suitable complete external pre-A1-to-C2 ladder has been identified. The project-defined equivalent must test listening, speaking, reading, and writing with published task shapes, rubrics, pass thresholds, and timed mocks; this mapping names the destination but does not claim that the current starter chapter reaches it.

sanskrit.caveat: Sanskrit is taught here as a living spoken language for the ramp's purposes, so CEFR's can-do descriptors apply. A traditional syllabus is ordered by grammar and text rather than by communicative function, so the two ladders are not parallel.

latin.caveat: CEFR is built around communicative can-do statements, and Latin is learned almost entirely for reading. A1 here means 'can greet, introduce oneself and read a short exchange', which keeps the shared spine usable across all 22 tracks; a reading-only ladder would fit Latin better and is worth revisiting.
